title: Regulation of Securities & Issuers
fullTitle: Regulation of Securities and Their Issuers

los.text: Identify instruments that are defined as securities under the Uniform Securities Act.
Recognize the securities exempt from registration under the Uniform Securities Act and the Securities Act of 1933.
Recall the exempt transactions under the Uniform Securities Act and the Securities Act of 1933.
Recollect the procedures for registering nonexempt securities under the Securities Act of 1933.
Recollect the procedures for registering nonexempt securities under the Uniform Securities Act.
Identify the methods of state registration of securities, including the antifraud provisions of the Uniform Securities Act.

concepts.subtopic: The USA, the Administrator, state vs. federal default
concepts.explanation: Federal law: Securities Act of 1933 (securities), Investment Advisers Act of 1940 (advisers), Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (broker-dealers). State law for all three: the Uniform Securities Act of 1956 (USA), model 'blue-sky' legislation that states adopt (the exam tests the 1956 USA as used by NASAA, not any particular state's law). 'State' includes the 50 states, territories (Guam, American Samoa, Virgin Islands), D.C. and Puerto Rico. When a question doesn't specify, the default is state law. The Administrator is the office or agency administering the state's securities law — registers securities and professionals, makes rules, issues orders, can deny/suspend/revoke registrations; jurisdiction over securities activity originating in or received in the state. Broker-dealers buy and sell securities for customers and their own accounts; agents (registered representatives) are the individuals representing them.
rules: Unspecified → state law (USA).
Administrator = the state securities regulator; very powerful but with limits.
misconceptions: Assuming a federal answer when the question is silent.

concepts.explanation: The USA applies only to securities. Under the Supreme Court's Howey test, an investment contract is a security if there is (1) an investment of money (2) in a common enterprise (3) with the expectation of profits (4) derived primarily from the efforts of others. The USA lists stocks, bonds, debentures, notes, collateral trust certificates, preorganization certificates, investment contracts, voting trust certificates, certificates of deposit for a security (ADRs — not bank CDs), oil/gas/mining interests, options on securities, warrants and rights, and 'anything commonly known as a security'. Easier: the six NON-securities — (1) insurance, endowment and fixed annuity contracts promising fixed sums (anything from a life insurer without 'variable'); (2) interests in retirement plans (IRA, 401(k)); (3) collectibles; (4) commodities, precious metals, grains, and futures/forwards; (5) a condominium used as a personal residence; (6) currency. Fraud in selling a nonsecurity is not a violation of securities law (other antifraud laws apply). A condo placed in a rental pool run by an agent IS a security (profit from others' efforts); a variable annuity IS a security.
rules: Howey: money, common enterprise, expected profit, from others' efforts.
Six nonsecurities: fixed insurance/annuity, retirement plan interests, collectibles, commodities/futures, residence condo, currency.
exceptions: Variable annuities and variable life are securities; fixed are not.
A condo in a rental pool is a security; a residence is not.
misconceptions: Treating a Treasury bond as a nonsecurity because it is exempt — exempt securities are still securities.

concepts.subtopic: Issuer; issuer vs. nonissuer transactions; IPO, primary, follow-on
concepts.explanation: An issuer is any person who issues or proposes to issue a security — mostly companies and governments. Oddity: for certificates of interest in oil, gas or mining titles/leases there is deemed to be no issuer. Issuer (primary) transaction: proceeds go to the issuer — every new issue; the first is the IPO; later ones are follow-on/additional primary offerings (APOs); mutual funds have a primary offering every day but only one IPO. Nonissuer (secondary) transaction: proceeds go to a selling investor — everyday exchange and Nasdaq trading. Follow the money.
rules: Proceeds to issuer = primary/issuer transaction. Proceeds to seller = secondary/nonissuer.
Only one IPO per issuer; many primary offerings possible.
exceptions: No issuer for oil/gas/mining interest certificates.
examples: State X sells bonds → issuer transaction; the buyer later resells through an agent → nonissuer transaction.
misconceptions: Calling the first trade between two investors OTC a 'primary transaction'.

concepts.explanation: A security is exempt because of the nature of its issuer, not the purchaser, and keeps its exemption at issue and in later trading (exemption from registration and from filing sales literature — never from antifraud). USA exempt securities: (1) U.S. and Canadian government and municipal securities — including political subdivisions (states/provinces, cities, counties)*; (2) foreign government securities of nations with U.S. diplomatic relations — but NOT their political subdivisions unless sovereign-guaranteed*; (3) depository institutions — banks, savings institutions, trust companies*, federal S&Ls, state building-and-loans and credit unions authorized to do business in the state; (4) insurance company securities (the company's stocks/bonds, NOT its variable products) if authorized in the state; (5) public utility and common carrier securities (incl. railroad equipment trust certificates) regulated as to rates or issuance; (6) nonprofit organizations — religious, educational, fraternal, charitable, social, athletic, reformatory, trade associations; (7) employee benefit plan investment contracts*; (8) certain money market instruments — commercial paper (≤ 9 months, ≥ $50,000 denominations, one of the top three ratings — the only place a rating matters under the USA) and banker's acceptances*. (*Marks the five cases where someone representing the issuer in a sale is excluded from the definition of agent — Unit 11.) The Administrator can revoke only two of these exemptions: nonprofits and employee benefit plans.
rules: Exempt security = exempt because of the issuer; retains exemption forever; still subject to antifraud.
USA commercial paper exemption: ≤ 270 days, ≥ $50,000, top-three rating.
Administrator may revoke only the nonprofit and employee-benefit-plan security exemptions.
exceptions: Foreign political subdivisions are not exempt (Canadian provinces/cities are).
Variable annuities and variable life are nonexempt even though the insurer's own stock is exempt.
examples: A $100,000 AAA promissory note maturing in 300 days is NOT exempt (over 270 days).
misconceptions: Treating a bank holding company's stock as exempt under federal law — the 1933 Act bank exemption excludes holding companies.

concepts.explanation: The National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 created federal covered securities (state registration preempted; only notice filings and fees allowed, mainly for investment companies) and federal covered advisers (Unit 9). Federal covered securities: (1) securities of investment companies registered under the 1940 Act (open-end, closed-end, UITs, FACs); (2) securities listed on the NYSE, NYSE American, Nasdaq Stock Market (and other named exchanges), plus securities equal or senior to them (rights, warrants, bonds, preferred); (3) securities sold under Rule 506(b) or 506(c) of Regulation D; (4) most securities exempt under the 1933 Act (Treasuries, municipals) — except a municipal bond is NOT federal covered in the issuer's own state (a Columbus, OH bond is federal covered everywhere but Ohio, where the Administrator may request details — it is still exempt there). SEC registration does not make a security federal covered (thousands of OTC/Pink stocks are SEC-registered but not covered), and a security need not be SEC-registered to be federal covered (Treasuries). States keep antifraud and licensing authority over sellers of federal covered securities.
rules: Federal covered: 1940 Act investment companies, exchange/Nasdaq-listed and senior/equal securities, Reg D 506, 1933-Act-exempt securities (muni exception in home state).
SEC-registered ≠ federal covered; federal covered ≠ SEC-registered.
Administrator cannot deny a federal covered security's transaction exemption or stop its sale absent fraud.
exceptions: Municipal bonds are not federal covered in the issuing state.
misconceptions: Assuming every SEC-registered stock is federal covered.

concepts.subtopic: Securities Act of 1933 exempted securities; Rules 147 and 147A
concepts.explanation: The 1933 Act exempts: U.S. government, state and municipal securities (NOT Canadian); commercial paper with maturity ≤ 270 days used for working capital, not fixed assets (no minimum denomination or rating, unlike the USA); nonprofit (religious, educational, benevolent, fraternal, charitable) securities; railroad equipment trust interests; securities of federal or state banks, S&Ls and building-and-loans — but NOT bank holding companies. Rule 147 (intrastate offering): exempt from federal registration (but generally must register with the state) when the entire issue is offered and sold only to residents of the one state where the issuer has its principal place of business (where officers/managers direct the business). Requirements: sales only to principal residents of the state; purchasers may resell only to in-state residents for six months from their purchase; issuer must reasonably believe and get a written representation of residency; a legend on the certificate; and at least one of — 80% of gross revenue from in-state operations, 80% of offering proceeds used in state, 80% of assets in state, or a majority of employees in state. One out-of-state sale kills the exemption for the whole issue. Rule 147A: same, except the issuer may be incorporated out of state (principal place of business must still be in state) and may make offers (general solicitation, internet) to out-of-staters — sales still only to residents.
rules: 1933 Act exempts U.S. govt/munis (not Canadian), ≤270-day commercial paper, nonprofits, railroad equipment trusts, banks (not holding companies).
Rule 147: in-state issuer and buyers; 80% revenue/proceeds/assets or majority of employees; six-month resale limit to out-of-staters.
147A adds: out-of-state incorporation OK; offers may go out of state; sales may not.
exceptions: A 147 purchaser may resell to a fellow resident at any time — the six-month limit applies only to sales to nonresidents.
examples: Incorporated in Delaware, headquartered in Idaho, selling only to Idahoans → Rule 147A, not 147.
misconceptions: Requiring 80% of employees in state — it is a majority.

concepts.explanation: An exempt transaction is exempt because of how or to whom the sale is made; the exemption must be established for each transaction, and the Administrator may deny any transaction exemption (except for federal covered securities) summarily. Burden of proving an exemption or exclusion is on the person claiming it. USA exempt transactions: isolated nonissuer transactions (infrequent person-to-person secondary sales without professionals); unsolicited brokerage transactions (client-initiated — the most common; Administrator may require the client to sign an acknowledgment form kept by the BD); underwriter transactions (issuer–underwriter and among syndicate members); transactions by an executor, administrator, sheriff, marshal, receiver, guardian or trustee in bankruptcy (not an UGMA/UTMA custodian; the only trustee is in bankruptcy); institutional investor transactions (banks, insurance companies, investment companies — no minimum size); limited offering (private placement) — no more than 10 OFFERS to noninstitutional persons in 12 months, buyers purchasing for investment, no commissions for soliciting noninstitutional buyers, no general advertising (the Administrator may change the 10); preorganization certificates — no commission, no more than 10 SUBSCRIBERS, no payment (may be advertised; postpones, does not excuse, registration); offers to existing security holders (incl. convertible, rights, warrant holders) with no commission for soliciting; nonissuer sales by a bona fide pledgee (lender selling collateral after default). Exemptions cover the security/transaction, not the professional — the seller must still be registered.
rules: USA private placement: 10 offerees (not purchasers) in 12 months, no retail commissions, no advertising.
Preorganization: 10 subscribers, no commission, no payment.
Fiduciary list: executor, administrator, sheriff, marshal, receiver, guardian, trustee in bankruptcy — not custodians.
Burden of proof on the claimant.
exceptions: Institutional transaction exemption has no minimum trade size.
Sale of nonexempt securities by a BD to a bank employee (an individual) is NOT exempt.
examples: A sale to 10 noninstitutional purchasers is not a USA private placement — the limit counts offers.
misconceptions: Counting purchasers instead of offerees under the USA (federal Rule 506 counts purchasers).

concepts.subtopic: 1933 Act exempt transactions: Regulation D Rule 506(b)/(c), accredited investors, Form D
concepts.explanation: Two federal exempt transactions: transactions by persons other than an issuer, underwriter or dealer (private trades between individuals) and issuer transactions not involving a public offering — Regulation D private placements. Rule 506 has no dollar limit; its securities are federal covered. 506(b): unlimited accredited investors plus up to 35 nonaccredited; no advertising. 506(c): general solicitation allowed if all purchasers are accredited (or reasonably believed so) and the issuer takes reasonable steps to verify (W-2s, tax returns, bank/brokerage statements, credit reports). 'Bad actor' disqualification: issuers or related persons convicted of securities fraud can't use 506. Accredited investors (Rule 501): banks, insurance companies, registered investment companies; employee benefit plans with a bank/insurer/RIA deciding or assets over $5 million; charities, corporations, LLCs, partnerships with assets over $5 million; directors, executive officers, general partners of the issuer; natural persons with net worth over $1 million (individually or with spouse/spousal equivalent) excluding the net equity in the primary residence; natural persons with income over $200,000 (or $300,000 joint) in each of the last two years with a reasonable expectation this year; entities of accredited investors; holders of Series 7, 65 or 82 licenses (for the 65, must actually be licensed as an IAR in the state); knowledgeable employees of private funds (only for that fund family); SEC- and state-registered advisers and exempt reporting advisers; entities with investments over $5 million. Jointly held assets with a non-spouse count only to the extent of the purchaser's share. Eligibility ≠ suitability. Form D must be filed electronically with the SEC within 15 days after the first sale.
rules: 506(b): ≤35 nonaccredited, no ads. 506(c): ads OK, all accredited and verified.
Accredited individual: $1M net worth ex-residence, or $200K/$300K income 2 years + expectation.
Form D: 15 days after first sale.
exceptions: Series 65 passers are accredited only if licensed as an IAR in their state.
misconceptions: Including the home's equity in net worth.
Treating accredited status as proof of suitability.

concepts.subtopic: Securities Act of 1933: registration statement, prospectus, SEC's role
concepts.explanation: The Securities Act of 1933 (Paper Act, Truth in Securities Act, Prospectus Act) requires full disclosure of material information for nonexempt securities sold in interstate commerce: file a registration statement, deliver a prospectus, and face civil/criminal/administrative penalties for violations and fraud. A prospectus is any written or broadcast communication offering a security or confirming a sale — not oral communications, and not a tombstone ad (security, price, underwriters only). An underwriter is any person (usually a BD) who buys from the issuer with a view to distribution or participates in it. The SEC does not approve securities, judge merit, or guarantee accuracy — it checks that disclosure is complete. The registration statement is signed by the CEO, CFO and a majority of the board, who face penalties for willful misstatements/omissions, and contains: purpose, anticipated price range, underwriter compensation, promotion expenses, use of proceeds, balance sheet, three years of earnings, names/bios of officers, directors, 10%+ holders and underwriters, the underwriting agreement, articles of incorporation.
rules: SEC never approves or guarantees; it reviews disclosure.
Signed by CEO, CFO, majority of directors.
Tombstone and oral statements are not prospectuses.

concepts.subtopic: Cooling-off period, red herring, effective date, final prospectus
concepts.explanation: Filing starts a cooling-off period of at least 20 calendar days (usually longer). Three phases: before filing — no solicitation, no prospectus; cooling-off — no sales, no orders, no money, no sales literature or advertising, but indications of interest (nonbinding on both sides), preliminary prospectuses and tombstone ads are allowed; after the effective date — sales may be solicited with the final prospectus. The preliminary (red herring) prospectus — named for the red legend on its cover — must be available to interested buyers from filing until effective; it gives essential facts and a bona fide estimated price range and expected share count but omits the final public offering price and the effective date; it cannot confirm a sale, replace the registration statement, or set the final price; no one may mark it up, summarize on it or highlight it. The final (effective) prospectus summarizes the registration statement and must be delivered to every purchaser no later than with the confirmation; sales literature may be used only if preceded or accompanied by a prospectus; no markings or highlighting on it either; money may now be accepted.
rules: Cooling-off: ≥ 20 days; indications of interest, red herrings, tombstones only.
Red herring lacks the final price and effective date.
Final prospectus to every buyer no later than the confirmation; never marked up.
examples: Agent whose client wants shares before the release date may send only the unaltered preliminary prospectus — no ads, no order request, no final prospectus.
misconceptions: Treating an indication of interest as binding on either side.

concepts.subtopic: USA registration statement contents, filers, fees, reports, stop orders
concepts.explanation: Under the USA it is unlawful to offer or sell a security in a state unless it is registered, the security or transaction is exempt, or it is a federal covered security. The registrant files with the Administrator: amount to be issued in the state; other states where offered (not amounts); any adverse order or judgment by a regulator, court or the SEC; anticipated effective date; anticipated use of proceeds. Documents filed within the last five years may be incorporated if still current; the Administrator may permit omissions. Filers: the issuer, a selling stockholder (e.g., an insider's block), or a broker-dealer — never the Administrator. Filing fee set by the Administrator (often a percentage of the offering); if withdrawn or stopped before effectiveness, part of the fee may be retained and the rest refunded. A stop order denies, suspends or revokes a securities registration (securities only — not professionals). Ongoing progress reports may be required, but not more often than quarterly. The Administrator may require sales on a specified subscription form, kept or filed for up to three years.
rules: Three lawful paths: registered, exempt (security or transaction), federal covered.
Reports no more than quarterly; stop orders apply to securities only.
Registration statements may be filed by the issuer, a selling shareholder, or a BD.
misconceptions: Listing the Administrator as a possible filer.

concepts.subtopic: Notice filing, coordination, qualification; effective dates; one-year life; amendments; escrow
concepts.explanation: Three state methods. Notice filing — for federal covered securities (mainly 1940 Act investment companies): the Administrator may require copies of SEC filings and amendments, a report of the value of securities offered in the state, a consent to service of process, and fees; limited review power; cannot block the sale absent fraud. Coordination — the most common method for non-covered securities (e.g., OTC/Pink stocks) when a 1933 Act registration is filed for the same offering: supply the latest prospectus, articles/bylaws/underwriting agreement/specimen certificate, other SEC filings on request, each prospectus amendment, and a consent to service; becomes effective simultaneously with the federal registration if no stop order or proceeding is pending, the filing has been on file the state's minimum (10–20 days), and the max/min offering price and underwriting discounts have been on file two business days. Qualification — any security; required when no other method fits (typically intrastate offerings and new companies): supply everything the Administrator asks (business description, 10%+ holders, use of proceeds, securities offered and costs, sales literature, specimen certificate, consent to service); effective when the Administrator so orders; the Administrator may require pre-sale prospectus delivery. A consent to service of process filed once need not be refiled. Every registration is effective for one year from its effective date, extendable while unsold shares are still offered at the original price. After effectiveness the share count may be increased by amendment if the offering price and underwriting discounts are unchanged. Under coordination or qualification the Administrator may require escrow of securities issued within three years, to promoters at a price substantially different from the offering, or for non-cash consideration, and may impound proceeds until a specified amount is raised.
rules: Notice filing: federal covered (investment companies). Coordination: with SEC registration; effective with the SEC. Qualification: anything; effective when the Administrator orders.
Registration lasts one year from the effective date.
Amend to add shares only if price and underwriting compensation are unchanged.
exceptions: A previously filed consent to service of process need not be refiled.
examples: A closed-end fund registered under the 1940 Act offering in four states → notice filing in each.
misconceptions: Thinking qualification's effective date is set by the SEC.

concepts.subtopic: Antifraud provisions reach everything that is a security
concepts.explanation: Fraud must be willful and knowing — there is no accidental fraud. The USA makes it unlawful, in connection with the offer, sale or purchase of any security, to employ a device or scheme to defraud, to make an untrue statement of material fact or omit one needed to make statements not misleading, or to engage in any practice that operates as a fraud; a parallel provision covers anyone paid for advice about securities. The antifraud provisions apply whether a security is registered, exempt, federal covered or sold in violation of registration — and to persons excluded from definitions (an engineer giving incidental advice, a federal covered adviser not registered in the state). The only escape is when the item is not a security at all: a rare-coin dealer falsifying dates or a fixed-annuity misstatement is fraud under other law, not the USA.
rules: Exempt from registration ≠ exempt from antifraud.
Exclusion from a definition ≠ exclusion from antifraud.
No security → no USA antifraud (but other laws apply).
misconceptions: Believing a federal covered adviser is beyond the state Administrator's reach for fraud.

lessons.title: The USA, what counts as a security, and who issues it
lessons.objective: Identify the governing laws and the Administrator, apply the Howey test and the six nonsecurities, and distinguish issuer (primary) from nonissuer (secondary) transactions.

blocks.b:
Federal: **Securities Act of 1933** (securities), **Investment Advisers Act of 1940** (advisers), **Securities Exchange Act of 1934** (broker-dealers). State, for all three: the **Uniform Securities Act of 1956 (USA)** — model 'blue-sky' legislation the states adopt. The exam tests the 1956 USA as NASAA uses it, not any one state's statute, and **when a question doesn't say, the answer is state law**.

'State' includes the 50 states, U.S. territories, D.C. and Puerto Rico.

The **Administrator** is the state office or agency that runs the securities law: registers securities and professionals, makes rules, issues orders, can deny, suspend or revoke registrations, with jurisdiction over activity originating in or received in the state. Powerful, with limits you'll learn in Unit 12. **Broker-dealers** trade for customers and themselves; **agents** are the individuals who represent them.

The USA covers only **securities**. The Supreme Court's **Howey test**: an **investment contract** is a security when there is (1) an **investment of money** (2) in a **common enterprise** (3) with the **expectation of profits** (4) **from the efforts of others**.

The USA lists dozens of instruments — stock, bonds, debentures, notes, collateral trust certificates, preorganization certificates, investment contracts, voting trust certificates, **certificates of deposit for a security (ADRs — not bank CDs)**, oil/gas/mining interests, options on securities, rights and warrants, anything commonly known as a security.

Easier: memorize the **six nonsecurities**:
1. **Insurance, endowment and fixed annuity contracts** promising fixed sums — any life-insurer product without the word *variable*.
2. **Interests in retirement plans** (IRA, 401(k)).
3. **Collectibles**.
4. **Commodities** — precious metals, grains — including **futures and forwards**.
5. A **condominium used as a personal residence**.
6. **Currency**.

Fraud in selling one of these isn't a securities-law violation (other laws apply). Watch the edges: a condo put in a **rental pool** run by an agent *is* a security (profit from others' efforts); a **variable** annuity *is* a security; a **Treasury bond** is a security (exempt from registration, but still a security).

An **issuer** is anyone who issues or proposes to issue a security — mostly companies and governments. (Odd but testable: for certificates of interest in oil, gas or mining leases, the USA says there is **no issuer**.)

- **Issuer (primary) transaction** — proceeds go to the **issuer**. Every new issue. The first is the **IPO**; later ones are **follow-on / additional primary offerings**. A mutual fund has a primary offering every day — but only one IPO.
- **Nonissuer (secondary) transaction** — proceeds go to a **selling investor**: everyday NYSE and Nasdaq trading.

Follow the money. If it lands with the issuer, it's primary.

lessons.title: Exempt securities: state, federal covered, and federal
lessons.objective: List the USA's exempt securities and which two the Administrator can revoke, define federal covered securities under NSMIA, list the 1933 Act exemptions, and apply Rules 147 and 147A.

blocks.b:
A security is exempt because of **who issued it**, not who buys it, and it stays exempt at issue and in every later trade. The exemption is from **registration and sales-literature filing** — never from antifraud.

1. **U.S. and Canadian** government and municipal securities — including states, provinces, cities, counties.*
2. **Foreign government** securities (nations with U.S. diplomatic relations) — but **not** their political subdivisions unless the sovereign guarantees them.*
3. **Depository institutions** — banks, savings institutions, trust companies*; federal S&Ls; state building-and-loans and credit unions authorized in the state.
4. **Insurance company** securities (the insurer's **own stock and bonds** — not its variable products) if authorized in the state.
5. **Public utility and common carrier** securities, including railroad equipment trust certificates, regulated as to rates or issuance.
6. **Nonprofit** organizations — religious, educational, fraternal, charitable, social, athletic, reformatory, trade associations.
7. **Employee benefit plan** investment contracts.*
8. Certain **money market instruments** — **commercial paper** (≤ 9 months, ≥ $50,000 denominations, one of the three highest ratings — the only time a rating matters under the USA) and banker's acceptances.*

*The five starred items are where a person selling for the issuer is not an 'agent' (Unit 11).

The Administrator can **revoke only two** security exemptions: **nonprofits** and **employee benefit plans**.

The **National Securities Markets Improvement Act** created **federal covered securities** — states may **not** require registration; they may only require **notice filings and fees** (mostly for investment companies). The categories:
- Securities of **investment companies registered under the 1940 Act** (open-end, closed-end, UITs, FACs).
- Securities **listed on the NYSE, NYSE American, the Nasdaq Stock Market** (and other named exchanges), plus anything **equal or senior** to them — rights, warrants, bonds, preferred.
- Securities sold under **Rule 506(b) or 506(c)** of Regulation D.
- Most securities **exempt under the 1933 Act** — Treasuries, municipals — with one twist: a **municipal bond is not federal covered in the issuer's own state**. A Columbus, OH bond is federal covered everywhere except Ohio, where the Administrator can ask the city for details (it is still exempt there).

Two traps: **SEC-registered does not mean federal covered** (thousands of OTC/Pink-sheet stocks are registered but not covered), and a security **need not be SEC-registered** to be covered (Treasuries). States keep **antifraud** and **licensing** authority over anyone selling covered securities.

blocks.h: Exempted securities under the Securities Act of 1933
blocks.b:
Similar list, important differences:
- U.S. government, state and municipal securities — **Canadian issues are NOT exempt** federally.
- **Commercial paper ≤ 270 days** used for working capital, not fixed assets — **no minimum denomination or rating** (unlike the USA).
- **Nonprofit** (religious, educational, benevolent, fraternal, charitable) securities.
- **Railroad equipment trust** interests.
- Securities of federal or state **banks**, S&Ls, building-and-loans — but **not bank holding companies** (which own most big banks today).

**Rule 147** exempts an offering from **federal** registration (it usually still registers with the **state**) when the **entire issue** is offered and sold **only to residents of the one state** where the issuer has its **principal place of business** (where officers and managers direct the business). Conditions:
- Sales only to people whose **principal residence** is in the state; the issuer must **reasonably believe** it and get a **written representation**; a **legend** on the certificate.
- Purchasers may resell to **out-of-state** buyers only after **six months** — resales to fellow residents are fine any time.
- At least **one** of: **80%** of gross revenue from in-state operations; **80%** of proceeds used in state; **80%** of assets in state; or a **majority of employees** in state.

**One sale to a nonresident kills the exemption for the whole issue.**

**Rule 147A** is the same except: the issuer may be **incorporated in another state** (principal place of business still in state), and it may make **offers** out of state — general solicitation, the internet — as long as **sales** go only to residents.

lessons.title: Exempt transactions: USA list and Regulation D
lessons.objective: Recall the USA's exempt transactions (and the 10-offeree private placement), the Administrator's power to deny them, and the federal Rule 506(b)/(c) private placement with the accredited-investor definition and Form D.

blocks.b:
A security is exempt because of its issuer (a *noun*); a transaction is exempt because of **how or to whom** it is sold (a *verb* — 'action'). Transaction exemptions must be established **each time**, the **Administrator may deny or revoke any of them** (summarily, without notice) **except** those involving **federal covered securities**, and the **burden of proof** is on whoever claims the exemption.

- **Isolated nonissuer transactions** — infrequent person-to-person secondary sales, no professionals involved (the 'for sale by owner' sign).
- **Unsolicited brokerage transactions** — **client-initiated**; the most common. The Administrator may require the client to sign an acknowledgment form the BD keeps.
- **Underwriter transactions** — issuer ↔ underwriter, and among syndicate members.
- Transactions by an **executor, administrator, sheriff, marshal, receiver, guardian, or trustee in bankruptcy**. Not an **UGMA/UTMA custodian**; the only trustee is one **in bankruptcy**.
- **Institutional investor** transactions — banks, insurance companies, investment companies; **no minimum size**.
- **Limited offering (private placement)** — no more than **10 offers** to noninstitutional persons in **12 months**; buyers purchase **for investment**; **no commissions** for soliciting retail buyers; **no general advertising**. The USA counts **offers**; federal law counts purchasers. The Administrator may raise or lower the 10.
- **Preorganization certificates** — **no commission**, no more than **10 subscribers**, **no payment** until registration (public advertising is allowed; this postpones rather than excuses registration).
- Offers to **existing security holders** (incl. convertible, rights and warrant holders) with no commission for soliciting.
- Nonissuer sales by a **bona fide pledgee** — the lender selling collateral after a default.

These exempt the security or transaction — **not the professional**. Whoever sells a Treasury bond still has to be registered to sell it.

A bank sells its bond portfolio to another bank: exempt (institutions). A BD buys from an issuer in a firm-commitment underwriting: exempt. A bank *employee* buys securities her agent recommended: **not** exempt — that's a BD selling to a member of the public.

The 1933 Act's testable exempt transactions: (1) transactions by anyone **other than an issuer, underwriter or dealer** — private trades between individuals; (2) issuer transactions **not involving a public offering** — **Regulation D**. **Rule 506** has **no dollar limit**, and its securities are **federal covered**.
- **506(b)** — unlimited **accredited** investors plus up to **35 nonaccredited**; **no advertising**.
- **506(c)** — **general solicitation allowed**, but **every purchaser must be accredited** (or reasonably believed so) and the issuer must take **reasonable steps to verify** (W-2s, tax returns, bank and brokerage statements, credit reports).
- **Bad actor** rule: issuers or related persons convicted of securities fraud can't use 506.
- **Form D** is filed electronically with the SEC within **15 days after the first sale**.

- Banks, insurance companies, registered investment companies.
- Employee benefit plans run by a bank, insurer or RIA, or with assets over **$5 million**.
- Charities, corporations, LLCs, partnerships — and almost any entity — with assets or investments over **$5 million**.
- **Directors, executive officers and general partners** of the issuer.
- Natural persons with **net worth over $1 million**, alone or with a spouse/spousal equivalent, **excluding the equity in the primary residence**.
- Natural persons with **income over $200,000** (or **$300,000 joint**) in each of the last **two years** and a reasonable expectation of the same this year.
- Entities made up of accredited investors.
- Holders of the **Series 7, 65 or 82** — for the 65, you must actually be **licensed as an IAR in your state**, not just have passed.
- **Knowledgeable employees** of a private fund — accredited only for that fund family.
- SEC-registered, state-registered and exempt reporting **investment advisers**.

Assets held jointly with a non-spouse count only to the extent of the purchaser's share. And **eligibility does not equal suitability** — meeting the test never waives suitability.

lessons.title: Registering with the SEC: the 1933 Act process
lessons.objective: Describe the registration statement and the SEC's limited role, define prospectus and underwriter, and apply the rules of the cooling-off period, red herring and final prospectus.

blocks.b:
The **Securities Act of 1933** (the Paper Act, Truth in Securities Act, Prospectus Act) requires issuers of nonexempt securities sold in interstate commerce to make **full disclosure of material information**: file a **registration statement**, deliver a **prospectus**, and face civil, criminal and administrative penalties for violations and fraud.

**The SEC does not approve securities, pass on their merit, or guarantee the accuracy of anything** — it only checks that disclosure is complete.

A **prospectus** is any written or broadcast communication that offers a security or confirms a sale. Not a prospectus: **oral** statements, and a **tombstone** ad (security, price, underwriters only). An **underwriter** is anyone — usually a BD — who buys from the issuer with a view to distribution or takes part in it.

The registration statement is signed by the **CEO, CFO and a majority of the board** (all liable for willful misstatements and omissions) and includes the purpose, anticipated price range, underwriter compensation, promotion expenses, use of proceeds, balance sheet, **three years** of earnings, names and bios of officers, directors, **10%+ holders** and underwriters, the underwriting agreement, and the articles of incorporation.

blocks.h: The three phases of an underwriting
rows: Indications of interest (nonbinding both ways), preliminary prospectus, tombstone ads
No orders, no money, no sales literature or advertising
Solicit sales with the final prospectus; accept money; sales literature if preceded or accompanied by a prospectus
No marking or highlighting the prospectus

blocks.b:
The **preliminary prospectus** gets its nickname from the **red-ink legend** on the cover saying the registration isn't yet effective. It must be made available to anyone who expresses interest from filing until the effective date. It gives the essential facts, the expected share count and a **bona fide estimated price range**, but **omits the final offering price and the effective date**. It cannot confirm a sale, substitute for the registration statement, or declare the final price — and nobody may write on it, summarize it, or highlight it.

The **final (effective) prospectus** summarizes the registration statement and must reach **every purchaser no later than with the confirmation**, whether or not they intend to read it. Same no-markings rule. Only now may money be accepted.

lessons.title: Registering with the state: three methods, and antifraud for all
lessons.objective: State what a USA registration statement contains and who may file it, distinguish notice filing, coordination and qualification with their effective dates, apply the one-year rule, amendments and escrow, and explain the reach of the antifraud provisions.

blocks.b:
Under the USA a security may be offered or sold in a state only if it is **registered**, the security or transaction is **exempt**, or it is **federal covered**.

The **registrant** files with the Administrator: the **amount** to be issued in the state; the **other states** where it will be offered (not the amounts); any **adverse order or judgment** by a regulator, court or the SEC; the **anticipated effective date**; the **use of proceeds**. Documents filed within the last **five years** may be incorporated if still current.

Who may file: the **issuer**, a **selling stockholder** (an insider unloading a block), or a **broker-dealer** — never the Administrator, who receives it. A **filing fee** (often a percentage of the offering) is set by the Administrator; if the registration is withdrawn or **stopped** before effectiveness, part may be kept and the rest refunded. A **stop order** denies, suspends or revokes a **securities** registration — it is never used against professionals. Progress **reports** may be required, but **no more often than quarterly**, and the Administrator may require a specified **subscription form** kept up to **three years**.

rows: Federal covered securities (mainly 1940 Act investment companies)
Securities also registering with the SEC (most non-covered multistate offerings, e.g., OTC/Pink)
Anything; required when no other method fits (intrastate, new companies)
SEC filings and amendments, value of securities offered in state, consent to service, fees
Latest prospectus, articles/bylaws/underwriting agreement/specimen certificate, other SEC filings on request, each amendment, consent to service
Whatever the Administrator requires: business, 10%+ holders, use of proceeds, costs, sales literature, specimen certificate, consent to service
On filing (limited review; can't block absent fraud)
Same moment as the SEC, if no stop order, on file 10–20 days, and price/discount info on file 2 business days

blocks.h: Life of a registration, amendments, escrow
blocks.b:
- A **consent to service of process** filed once need not be filed again (a new job, a new offering).
- Every registration is effective for **one year from its effective date** — and may run longer while unsold shares are still offered at the **original price**.
- After effectiveness, the **number of shares** may be increased by amendment if the **offering price and underwriting discounts are unchanged**.
- Under coordination or qualification the Administrator may require **escrow** of securities issued within the past **three years**, issued to a **promoter** at a substantially different price, or issued for **non-cash** consideration — and may **impound proceeds** until a target amount is raised, so the issuer can't take the money and run.

blocks.h: Antifraud reaches everything that is a security
blocks.b:
Fraud is always **willful and knowing** — there is no accidental fraud. The USA makes it unlawful, in connection with any offer, sale or purchase of a security, to use a scheme to defraud, to make an **untrue statement of material fact** or **omit** one needed to keep statements from being misleading, or to engage in any practice that operates as a fraud; a parallel rule covers anyone paid for advice about securities.

The provisions apply whether the security is **registered, exempt, federal covered, or sold illegally** — and to people **excluded from definitions**: an engineer giving incidental advice can commit advisory fraud; a **federal covered adviser** not registered in the state can be charged by the state Administrator.

The only way out is for the thing **not to be a security**: a rare-coin dealer faking dates, or a misstatement selling a **fixed annuity**, is fraud — under other laws, not the USA.

questions.stem: On the Series 65 exam, the term 'Administrator' refers to
options: the SEC commissioner responsible for a region.
the state office or agency responsible for administering the state's securities laws.
FINRA's district director.
the chief compliance officer of a broker-dealer.
questions.explanation: The Administrator is the state securities regulator with authority over registration of securities and professionals, rulemaking, and enforcement in the state.
why: The Administrator is a state official.
FINRA is a federal SRO.
A firm's CCO is not the Administrator.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a security under the Uniform Securities Act?
options: A fixed annuity contract
An interest in a 401(k) plan
A variable annuity contract
A commodity futures contract
questions.explanation: A variable annuity's value depends on securities in a separate account, so it is a security. Fixed annuities, retirement plan interests and futures are among the six nonsecurities.
why: Fixed insurance products are not securities.
Retirement plan interests are not securities.
Commodities and futures are not securities.

questions.stem: An investor buys a resort condominium and places it in a rental pool managed by a rental agent, using it personally only two weeks a year. Under the Howey test, the condominium interest is
options: not a security, because real estate is never a security.
a security, because profit is expected from the efforts of a third party.
not a security, because the investor occasionally occupies it.
a security only if it is registered with the SEC.
questions.explanation: Money invested in a common enterprise (the pool) with profits expected from the rental agent's efforts meets Howey. A condo used as a personal residence would not be a security.
why: An investment contract can involve real estate.
Occasional personal use does not change the profit motive and reliance on others.
Registration status does not define a security.

questions.stem: An agent commits fraud in the sale of rare coins to a client. Under the Uniform Securities Act, the agent
options: has violated the antifraud provisions of the act.
has not violated the act because collectibles are not securities, though other laws may apply.
must be registered as a dealer in collectibles.
has violated the act only if the coins were unregistered.
questions.explanation: The USA applies only to securities; collectibles are not securities. The fraud is actionable under other commercial laws.
why: The USA's antifraud provisions require a security.
No such requirement under the USA.
Collectibles cannot be registered as securities.

questions.stem: A transaction in which the proceeds of the sale go to the company that originally issued the security is
options: a nonissuer transaction.
a secondary transaction.
an issuer (primary) transaction.
an isolated transaction.
questions.explanation: When the issuer receives the proceeds, it is a primary or issuer transaction; secondary trading sends proceeds to the selling investor.
why: Nonissuer means the issuer gets nothing.
Secondary trading is between investors.
An isolated transaction is a type of nonissuer transaction.

questions.stem: Which statement about initial public offerings is correct?
options: A mutual fund conducts an IPO every business day.
An issuer may have only one IPO but may conduct additional primary offerings later.
Secondary trading on the NYSE is part of the IPO.
The proceeds of an IPO go to the underwriters' clients.
questions.explanation: The IPO is the first distribution to the public; later new-share sales are follow-on or additional primary offerings. Mutual funds have a continuous primary offering but only one IPO.
why: Funds have daily primary offerings, not daily IPOs.
Exchange trading is secondary.
IPO proceeds go to the issuer.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an exempt security under the Uniform Securities Act?
options: Bonds issued by the Province of Ontario
Stock of an insurance company authorized to do business in the state
A variable annuity issued by an insurance company authorized to do business in the state
Debt of a railroad regulated as to rates by a federal authority
questions.explanation: The insurer's own stock is exempt; its variable products are nonexempt securities that must register. Canadian provinces and regulated common carriers are exempt.
why: Canadian political subdivisions are exempt under the USA.
Insurance company securities are exempt.
Common carrier securities regulated as to rates are exempt.

questions.stem: Commercial paper is exempt from registration under the Uniform Securities Act if it
options: matures within 270 days, is issued in denominations of at least $50,000, and carries one of the three highest ratings.
matures within one year and is issued by a bank.
is sold only to accredited investors.
is guaranteed by the issuer's parent company.
questions.explanation: The USA's money market exemption requires maturity within nine months, minimum $50,000 denominations, and a top-three rating — the only instance where a rating affects a USA exemption.
why: The limit is nine months, and the issuer is a corporation.
Accredited investor status relates to Regulation D.
A guarantee does not create the exemption.

questions.stem: The Administrator may, by rule or order, deny or revoke the registration exemption of securities issued by
options: the U.S. Treasury.
a bank organized under state law.
a nonprofit charitable organization.
a regulated public utility.
questions.explanation: Only two security exemptions may be revoked: nonprofit organizations and employee benefit plans. Government, bank and utility exemptions cannot be denied.
why: Cannot be revoked.
Cannot be revoked.
Cannot be revoked.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a federal covered security?
options: Shares of a mutual fund registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940
Common stock listed on the Nasdaq Stock Market
Common stock registered with the SEC and quoted on the OTC Pink market
Securities sold under Rule 506(b) of Regulation D
questions.explanation: SEC registration alone does not make a security federal covered; OTC/Pink-market stocks must still register with the state (usually by coordination). Investment companies, Nasdaq-listed stocks and Rule 506 offerings are federal covered.
why: Federal covered.
Federal covered.
Federal covered.

questions.stem: A general obligation bond issued by the City of Austin, Texas, is
options: a federal covered security in every state, including Texas.
a federal covered security in every state except Texas, where it remains an exempt security.
a nonexempt security that must register by coordination in Texas.
exempt only under federal law.
questions.explanation: Under NSMIA, a municipal security is not federal covered in the issuer's home state, though it is still exempt there; the Texas Administrator may request details about the issue.
why: The home-state exception applies.
Municipal bonds are exempt securities under the USA.
It is exempt under both state and federal law.

questions.stem: With respect to a federal covered security, a state Administrator may
options: require registration by qualification.
require a notice filing and the payment of a fee.
prohibit its sale in the state because of the issuer's weak financial condition.
deny the exemption for an unsolicited transaction in that security.
questions.explanation: NSMIA preempts state registration of federal covered securities; states may require notice filings and fees (and enforce antifraud and licensing), but cannot block sales absent fraud or deny transaction exemptions involving covered securities.
why: Registration is preempted.
No merit review of covered securities.
Transaction exemptions in federal covered securities cannot be denied.

questions.stem: Which of the following is exempt from registration under the Securities Act of 1933?
options: Bonds issued by the government of Canada
Stock of a bank holding company
Commercial paper maturing in 180 days used to finance inventory
Shares of a closed-end fund
questions.explanation: Commercial paper with maturity of 270 days or less used for working capital is exempt federally. Canadian securities and bank holding companies are not exempt under the 1933 Act; investment company shares register with the SEC.
why: Canadian issues are exempt under the USA but not the 1933 Act.
The bank exemption excludes holding companies.
Investment companies register under federal law.

questions.stem: To qualify for the Rule 147 intrastate exemption, an issuer must meet at least one of the following EXCEPT
options: 80% of gross revenue derived from operations within the state.
80% of the offering proceeds used within the state.
80% of its employees located within the state.
80% of its assets located within the state.
questions.explanation: The employee test is a majority of employees, not 80%. The three 80% tests cover revenue, proceeds and assets.
why: A valid test.
A valid test.
A valid test.

questions.stem: Three months ago a client bought shares in a Rule 147 offering. She now wants to sell them. Which statement is correct?
options: She may sell to a resident of her state now, but may not sell to a nonresident until six months after her purchase.
She must hold the shares for six months before any resale.
She may sell to anyone immediately because the exemption covers only the issuer.
She must sell through the original underwriter.
questions.explanation: The six-month resale restriction applies only to sales to residents of other states; in-state resales are permitted at any time.
why: In-state resales are not restricted.
Out-of-state resales within six months are barred.
No such requirement.

questions.stem: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following is an exempt transaction?
options: An agent recommends and sells nonexempt securities to an individual client.
A customer calls her agent and asks to buy shares of an unregistered nonexempt security.
An issuer sells shares to 15 retail investors through a public advertisement.
A custodian under UTMA sells securities in the minor's account.
questions.explanation: An unsolicited brokerage transaction — initiated by the client — is exempt. A solicited retail sale is not; a public offering to 15 retail investors exceeds the private placement limits; UTMA custodians are not on the fiduciary list.
why: Solicited sales to the public are nonexempt.
Exceeds 10 offerees and uses advertising.
Custodians are not among the exempt fiduciaries.

questions.stem: A limited offering (private placement) is an exempt transaction under the Uniform Securities Act if, among other conditions,
options: no more than 10 purchases are made by noninstitutional investors in 12 months.
no more than 10 offers are made to noninstitutional persons in 12 consecutive months.
no more than 35 nonaccredited investors purchase.
all purchasers are accredited investors.
questions.explanation: The USA limits offers (not purchases) to 10 noninstitutional persons per 12 months, with no retail commissions, no advertising, and purchase for investment. The 35-purchaser figure is federal Rule 506(b).
why: The USA counts offers, not purchases.
That is Regulation D.
Accredited status is a federal concept.

questions.stem: Under the Uniform Securities Act, the burden of proving that a security or transaction qualifies for an exemption rests with
options: the Administrator.
the person claiming the exemption.
the SEC.
the purchaser.
questions.explanation: Whoever claims an exemption or an exclusion from a definition must prove it.
why: The Administrator does not prove exemptions for registrants.
The SEC is not involved in USA exemptions.
Purchasers do not bear the burden.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about the Administrator's power over exemptions is correct?
options: The Administrator may revoke any securities exemption but no transaction exemption.
The Administrator may revoke any transaction exemption except those involving federal covered securities, and only two securities exemptions.
The Administrator may not revoke any exemption without a hearing.
The Administrator may revoke exemptions only with SEC approval.
questions.explanation: Transaction exemptions (other than in federal covered securities) may be denied summarily; only the nonprofit and employee-benefit-plan security exemptions may be revoked.
why: Reversed.
Transaction exemptions may be denied summarily, without prior notice.
No SEC approval is required.

questions.stem: The principal difference between Rule 506(b) and Rule 506(c) of Regulation D is that
options: 506(b) permits general solicitation; 506(c) does not.
506(c) permits general solicitation if all purchasers are accredited and verified; 506(b) allows up to 35 nonaccredited purchasers but no advertising.
506(b) has a $5 million limit; 506(c) has no limit.
only 506(c) offerings are federal covered securities.
questions.explanation: 506(c) trades the ability to advertise for an all-accredited, verified investor base; 506(b) forbids advertising but admits up to 35 nonaccredited investors. Neither has a dollar limit; both are federal covered.
why: Reversed.
Rule 506 has no dollar limit.
Both are federal covered.

questions.stem: A married couple has joint income of $280,000 in each of the last two years and a net worth of $1.4 million, of which $600,000 is the equity in their home. For a Rule 506 offering, they
options: are accredited under the income test.
are accredited under the net worth test.
are not accredited under either test.
are accredited because they own their home outright.
questions.explanation: Joint income must exceed $300,000 ($280,000 fails); net worth excluding primary-residence equity is $800,000, below $1 million. Eligibility also would not have established suitability.
why: $280,000 joint is below the $300,000 threshold.
$1.4M − $600K home equity = $800K.
Home equity is excluded.

questions.stem: An issuer relying on Regulation D must file Form D with the SEC
options: before any offers are made.
no later than 15 days after the first sale.
within 30 days after the offering closes.
only if nonaccredited investors participate.
questions.explanation: Rule 503 requires electronic filing of Form D within 15 days after the first sale of securities in the offering.
why: Filing follows the first sale.
The deadline runs from the first sale, not the close.
Form D is required for all Reg D offerings.

questions.stem: Which statement about accredited investor status is correct?
options: An investor who meets the accredited investor test is automatically suitable for any private placement.
A person who has passed the Series 65 is accredited regardless of licensing.
A director or executive officer of the issuer is an accredited investor for that issuer's offering.
Net worth includes the full value of the investor's primary residence.
questions.explanation: Directors, executive officers and general partners of the issuer are accredited. Eligibility never equals suitability; Series 65 status requires actual IAR licensing; primary-residence equity is excluded.
why: Regulators stress that eligibility does not equal suitability.
NASAA requires licensing as an IAR, not merely passing.
Home equity is excluded from net worth.

questions.stem: Under the Securities Act of 1933, the SEC's review of a registration statement
options: approves the security for sale to the public.
guarantees the accuracy of the prospectus.
attempts to ensure full disclosure of material information but does not pass on investment merit.
certifies that the offering price is fair.
questions.explanation: The SEC neither approves securities nor guarantees statements; it reviews for complete disclosure. Claiming SEC approval is unlawful.
why: The SEC never approves.
No guarantee of accuracy.
No pricing judgment.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a prospectus under the Securities Act of 1933?
options: A letter offering a security for sale
A television broadcast offering a security
A tombstone advertisement identifying the security, price and underwriters
A written confirmation of a sale
questions.explanation: A prospectus is any written or broadcast communication offering or confirming a sale; tombstone ads and oral communications are excluded.
why: A written offer is a prospectus.
Broadcast offers are prospectuses.
Confirmations of sale fall within the definition.

questions.stem: During the cooling-off period, an underwriter may
options: accept orders and payment for the new issue.
distribute sales literature promoting the issue.
distribute the preliminary prospectus and take nonbinding indications of interest.
deliver the final prospectus with the offering price.
questions.explanation: Before the effective date, only indications of interest, red herrings and tombstone ads are permitted; no orders, money, sales literature or final prospectus.
why: Orders and money may not be accepted until effective.
Sales literature is barred during cooling-off.
The final prospectus does not exist until the effective date.

questions.stem: Two items missing from a preliminary (red herring) prospectus are
options: the issuer's name and the underwriters.
the final public offering price and the effective date.
the use of proceeds and the balance sheet.
the number of shares and the estimated price range.
questions.explanation: The red herring shows an estimated price range and expected share count but not the final price or the effective date, which are unknown until the SEC releases the issue.
why: Both are included.
Both are disclosed.
Both are included (the range, not the final price).

questions.stem: After the effective date, an agent sells shares of a new issue to a customer. The final prospectus must be delivered
options: only if the customer requests it.
no later than with the confirmation of the sale.
within 30 days of settlement.
only to customers who did not receive a red herring.
questions.explanation: Every purchaser must receive the final prospectus no later than with the confirmation, whether or not they intend to read it.
why: Delivery is mandatory.
Too late.
All purchasers receive it.

questions.stem: A registration statement for a securities offering in a state may be filed by all of the following EXCEPT
options: the issuer.
a selling stockholder holding a large block.
a broker-dealer.
the state Administrator.
questions.explanation: The Administrator receives registration statements; issuers, selling shareholders and broker-dealers may file them.
why: May file.
May file.
May file.

questions.stem: Under the Uniform Securities Act, the Administrator may require the person who filed a securities registration statement to file progress reports
options: monthly.
no more often than quarterly.
weekly during the offering period.
only after the offering is complete.
questions.explanation: Reports to keep the registration current may be required, but not more often than quarterly.
why: Too frequent.
Too frequent.
Reports track the progress of the offering.

questions.stem: An open-end investment company registered under the Investment Company Act of 1940 intends to offer shares in a state. The state may require
options: registration by coordination.
registration by qualification.
a notice filing with a fee and consent to service of process.
nothing, because federal covered securities are beyond state authority entirely.
questions.explanation: Investment company securities are federal covered; states cannot require registration but may require notice filings, fees, and a consent to service of process, and retain antifraud authority.
why: Coordination is for securities registering with the SEC that are not federal covered.
Qualification is not available for covered securities.
States may require notice filings and enforce antifraud rules.

questions.stem: A registration by qualification becomes effective
options: simultaneously with the SEC registration.
20 days after filing.
when the Administrator so orders.
upon payment of the filing fee.
questions.explanation: Qualification is the only method where the Administrator sets the effective date; coordination becomes effective with the federal registration.
why: That is coordination.
No automatic period applies.
Fees alone do not create effectiveness.

questions.stem: Which statement about a state securities registration is correct?
options: It is effective for one year from the effective date, and the share amount may be increased by amendment if the price and underwriting discounts are unchanged.
It is effective for one year from January 1 of the filing year.
It expires automatically when the offering is 50% sold.
It may be amended to raise the offering price without a new filing.
questions.explanation: Registrations last one year from effectiveness (longer while unsold shares are offered at the original price), and the quantity may be increased post-effectiveness only if the price and underwriting compensation are unchanged.
why: It runs from the effective date.
No such rule.
A price change is not permitted by simple amendment.

questions.stem: As a condition of registration by qualification or coordination, the Administrator may require escrow of securities
options: issued to the public at the offering price.
issued within the past three years, issued to a promoter at a substantially different price, or issued for consideration other than cash.
of any issuer with fewer than 100 shareholders.
sold only to accredited investors.
questions.explanation: Escrow may be required for recently issued, promoter-priced, or non-cash-consideration securities; proceeds may also be impounded until a minimum is raised.
why: Ordinary public shares are not the target.
No shareholder-count test.
Not related to accredited status.

questions.stem: The antifraud provisions of the Uniform Securities Act apply to
options: only securities registered in the state.
all securities, whether registered, exempt, federal covered or sold in violation of registration requirements.
only nonexempt securities and the professionals who sell them.
fixed annuities and rare coins as well as securities.
questions.explanation: Exemption from registration is never exemption from antifraud; the provisions reach every security and every person involved. Nonsecurities such as fixed annuities and coins fall under other laws.
why: Registration status is irrelevant.
Exempt securities and excluded persons are covered too.
Nonsecurities are outside the USA.

questions.stem: A federal covered investment adviser, not registered in State A, makes fraudulent statements to a State A resident about a security. The State A Administrator
options: has no jurisdiction because the adviser is federal covered.
may bring an action under the antifraud provisions of the USA.
may act only if the security is registered in State A.
must refer the matter to the SEC and take no action.
questions.explanation: Federal covered status preempts state registration, not state antifraud authority; the Administrator may pursue fraud by any person in connection with securities.
why: Antifraud jurisdiction is retained.
Registration of the security is irrelevant to fraud.
The state may act on its own.

questions.front: Default law when the exam doesn't specify; the Administrator
questions.back: State law — the Uniform Securities Act (1956, as NASAA uses it). The Administrator = the state agency administering securities law; registers, makes rules, issues orders, can deny/suspend/revoke.

Money + common enterprise + expected profit + from others' efforts. Not securities: fixed insurance/annuity/endowment, retirement plan interests, collectibles, commodities & futures, residence condo, currency.
Issuer (primary): proceeds to the issuer (IPO, follow-on, daily mutual fund sales). Nonissuer (secondary): proceeds to a selling investor (exchange trading).

questions.front: USA exempt securities (list) and the two the Administrator can revoke
questions.back: U.S./Canadian govt & munis; foreign govts (not subdivisions); banks/S&Ls/credit unions; insurer securities; utilities/common carriers; nonprofits; employee benefit plans; commercial paper (≤9 mo, ≥$50K, top-3 rating). Revocable: nonprofits, employee benefit plans.

1940 Act investment companies; NYSE/NYSE American/Nasdaq-listed + equal/senior securities; Reg D 506 offerings; 1933-Act-exempt securities — except munis in their home state. SEC-registered ≠ federal covered.

Both: in-state principal place of business, sales only to residents, 80% revenue/proceeds/assets or majority of employees, 6-month resale limit to nonresidents. 147A adds: incorporate elsewhere OK; offers may go out of state.

questions.front: USA private placement and preorganization certificate limits
questions.back: Private placement: ≤10 OFFERS to noninstitutional persons in 12 months, no retail commissions, no advertising, buy for investment. Preorganization: ≤10 SUBSCRIBERS, no commission, no payment (ads OK).

questions.front: 506(b) vs. 506(c); accredited individual tests; Form D
questions.back: 506(b): ≤35 nonaccredited, no ads. 506(c): ads OK, all accredited + verified. Individual: >$1M net worth ex-home, or $200K/$300K income 2 yrs + expectation. Form D ≤15 days after first sale.

questions.front: What the SEC does NOT do; who signs the registration statement
questions.back: Does not approve, judge merit, or guarantee accuracy — reviews disclosure only. Signed by CEO, CFO, majority of directors.

Allowed: indications of interest (nonbinding), red herring, tombstone. Prohibited: orders, money, sales literature/ads, final prospectus. Red herring lacks final price and effective date; never mark it up.

questions.front: Who may file a state registration statement; report frequency; stop order scope
questions.back: Issuer, selling stockholder, or broker-dealer (never the Administrator). Reports ≤ quarterly. Stop orders apply to securities registrations only.

questions.front: Notice filing / coordination / qualification — use and effective date
questions.back: Notice filing: federal covered (investment companies), fees. Coordination: with SEC filing, effective with SEC (on file 10–20 days, price info 2 business days). Qualification: anything, effective when the Administrator orders. All last 1 year from effectiveness.

questions.front: Who/what escapes the USA antifraud provisions?
questions.back: Only things that are not securities (fixed annuity, rare coins). Exempt securities, federal covered securities, and persons excluded from definitions are all still covered. Fraud must be willful.

terms.def: Rule 501 investor eligible for Reg D private placements — institutions, insiders, $1M net worth ex-home, $200K/$300K income, certain licensees.
The state office or agency administering the state's securities law.
State securities laws; the Uniform Securities Act is their model.
Filing that lets the Administrator receive legal papers on the registrant's behalf; filed once, not refiled.
At least 20 days after filing with the SEC before a registration can become effective.
NSMIA category preempting state registration — investment companies, listed securities, Reg D 506, 1933-Act-exempt securities.
